header.label: projects
header.title: Autogear: Learning to Shift Without a Torque Sensor
header.lede: An automatic derailleur for ordinary bikes, without a torque sensor. We built the hardware; I built the model that chooses the gear: 100 boosted trees and a hysteresis controller that, in closed-loop simulation, beat a decision table given the torque, and fit in 14.9 KB of flash on the box's Arduino.

decisionGroup.label: the R&D choices in detail
decisionGroup.open: ↓ the R&D choices in detail, with their math

decisions.title: No torque sensor, by design
decisions.caption: Two decision tables fitted to the riders: a target cadence c* (rpm) from the slope s, without and with the pedalling power P = torque × angular velocity. Adding P moves agreement within one gear from 80.4 % to 80.8 %.

decisions.title: Rebuild the rides that were never recorded
decisions.caption: Gear recovery, simplified (the full cost also caps the first term and adds a penalty for jumps of several gears). d = 60 v / c: the measured development; L_g: the gear levels found in the ride; σ = 0.05, λ = 15; solved with the Viterbi algorithm.

decisions.title: Predict the gear, not the shift
decisions.caption: L(g): development of gear g, in metres per crank turn; g*: the rider's gear; z(t): the 14 inputs; H = 3 s. The controller C shifts one step once the target has stayed beyond the dead band for k = 3 s.

decisions.title: Judged in closed loop, not offline
decisions.caption: Closed-loop replay: c, the recorded cadence; g*, the rider's gear; g^P, the gear the policy chose. Speed is held fixed, which is sound while the policy stays close to the rider.

decisions.title: A model that fits on the board
decisions.caption: Each tree f_k is stored as a complete binary tree of depth 4 (unused branches padded), so every decision costs exactly the same, whatever the input. η = 0.1.
